Church and State.


ROME, December 23.-The reception at
the Vatican today was largely attended by
Catholic Church dignitaries. Replying to
the Christmas greetings the pope deplored
the conflict between the state and the holy
see, which impartial minds desired to end.
The minority of Italians, his holiness con-
tinued, were against it and it was wrong
to fight the will of the people, who under
stood that the political unity did not suf-
flee to give them prosperity.


Therefore they desired the independence
of the papacy and the restoration of its
rights. Peaceful citizens should not be
COMPOUNDED with the subversive factions
whose aim was to set the cause of Italy
and the rights Of the papacy in conflict. 1t
had never been unworthy, and the state
should make just reparatiOn.


The pope, who was in excellent health
and splendid voice, blessed all present, in
GLIDING twentythree cardinals. Afterward,
every guest passed the throne of the pope
and his holiness said few words to ZACH
of them.

attention. He was native of Lawrence

fugitive's clothes and took his place in

away in Porter's clothing. The next morn
ing the court ordered the supposed fugitive
brought forward for Identification, only to
find that the authorities had been neatly
trapped. Instead of the slave young Porter
occupied the cell, looking natty and neat,
having washed off his burnt cork and
otherwise cleansed himself. The trick
aroused intense excitement, and the SYM
pathizers with slavery threatened all sorts
of revenge, but no prosecution ever came
of it.

The Wife or Senator Platt's Private Secretary


Interested In Her Behalf


Gerry Agent Thomas Watson found q woman
soliciting aims at Broadway and Twenty sec
ond street yesterday afternoon. Tho woman
held by the hand her 4.year-old daughter, and
many passersby handed the child money. Agent
Watson hailed the mother and child to the West
Thirtieth street station house. where the wo-
man described herself as Mrs. Annie Frank, 80
years old, OF 231 East Twenty-fourth street.


While on the way to the station three well.
dressed women inquired the cause of Mrs.
Franks arrest. When they learned that she
had been ARE 'ted for begging they accom-
panied her to the police station and pleaded for
her release, saying that they would see that
mother and child were properly cared for.
Agent Watson would not consent to their re-
lease, however, and Mrs. Frank was locked up.
Her child was taken to the Gerry socieiy's
headquarters.


One OF the women who interested herself in
Mrs. Frank was Mrs. Morris Eckstein, wife of
Senator Platt's private secretary. Mrs. Eek
stein said she would appear in Jefferson Mar.
ket Court this morning, when Mrs. Frank was
arraigned, and ask to be allowed to aid her.
Mrs. Frank has two children. Her husband
hasn't worked in two years. She says he can't
get work and that she had to beg TO keep the
family from starving.

In the estate of Emmett NJ. Hickey, de-
ceased, Judge Coffey has handed down
written opinion setting forth the reasons
for vacating former order settling the
account of the administrator.


Hickey had been married twice and
both times divorced. Mary Cummings,
formerly Mary Hickey, the woman who
was his first wife, presented claim for
$3.50 for alimony, but this was compro-
missed for $400, and it's payment was al
lowed, and 1t was included in the admins
traitors account as settled by the court.
Mary Hickey, the second divorced wife,
applied for family allowance as widow
of the decedent, on the ground that the
decree had not been signed.


Subsequently an attorney was appointed
to represent the absent minor heirs, and
thev by their attorney objected to the pay
ment of the $400 to Mrs. Mary Hickey
Cummings on the ground that they were
not notified of her application, as was
their right.


Judge Coffey heard argument on this
point and finally decided that the position
taken by the minor heirs was correct, and
set aside the settlement of the admins
traitors account. This opens up the mat
ters OF the entire estate and gives both
divorced women and their children an
other opportunity to enter the struggle
for the estate.

What apparently was a case of premedi-

here last night. On the night of June ~

refused to leave the spot until the body
was recovered. Afterward the dog acted
as guard over the body and moaned and

deepest melancholia.


Last night Tip ran through the saloon
and club room, above. which Madison fire.
quented. barking and looking for his mas
ter. Finally he ran Gp the stairs to the
fiat roof of the building. stood squarely
upon the edge of the roof and ieaped to
the brick-paved street below. The fall
broke his back and bystanders who watch
ed the proceedings with the greatest con-
cern put him cut Of his pain.

able in life. and It is believed by many
that the dog deliberately ended his own
life because his load of grief was greater
than he could bear.

Louis and Benjamin Tollin and Ar.
thur and Raymond Elliott wandered
away from home yesterday morning.


The Tollin boys are aged six and -four
years, respectively, and the Elliott
youngsters counted exactly the same
number OF years to their credit. About
II o'clock the Tollin boys asked per.
mission to 60 out and play with some Of
the children in the neighborhood.


Abraham Tollin, the father, granted
permission and the boys disappeared.


They did not come home to dinner,
and the parents becoming anxious went
around the neighborhood searching for
them, but no trace Of the boys could be
found. During the search it was found
that the Elliott children were also miss.
ing. The parents were nearly frantic,
and it was feared that the youngsters
had been kidnapped.


The neighbors joined in the search
and the police were notified, and in a
very short time the city was being thor

All efforts to find them were without re-
suit until nearly dark when Mr.. Tollin's
brother, who had taken the southern
portion of the city as his territory, found
the quartet n Maryland avenue.

a miserable little crowd. Their tear
stained faces and hands red and swollen
with cold bore evidence that the fun OF
running away had long since vanished


They were taken home to their moth.
ers and between sobs they tried to tell
the story of their wanderings. So tired
and, excited were they, however, that
nothing definite could be learned, ex-

Few spots in the United Kingdom are
possessed Of more romantic interest than
Gretna Green, on the Scottish Dor.
der. where, according to local rec.
ords, more than 10000 runaway mar
riages have been celebrated. According to
Scotch law, says the New York World, an
acknowledgment before witnesses that q
woman was ones wife constituted legal
marriage, and SO runaway couples made
their way from all parts of England to
Gretna Green, where they would acknowl-
edge them selves to be man and wife at the
smitny in the presence of the blacksmith,
who would take his position behind the
anvil, repeat short prayer and give them
his blessing and a certificate.


Some time ago an act of Parliament was
passed forbidding these Gretna Gree n
marriages unless the parties had resided
three weeks in Scotland, and Great Brit
ain marriages will soon be thing of the
past. William Lang died recently. Old
Lang, who recently celebrated his eigh-
tieth birthday, was the last of four gen.
erations of these marrying blacksmiths.
Among those who have been welded by
the Langs have been the Earl OF Dundon-
aid, who eloped over the border with
Miss Barnes, and Lord Erstine, who
posted all the way from London to the
Scottish border with Sarah Buck.


The smithy stands within five minutes
walk from the bridge which marks the
line between the two kingdoms and looks
on Gretna Green, an open, verdant space
surrounded by few one.storied ancient
cottages. Few tourists ever visit the ro-
mantle spot, which figures in the guide
book and possesses no hotel. and yet
which is associated with the thrilling adj
ventures and marvellous escapes OF some
10000 English lovers of the aristocracy
and the wealthy classes.

caust. The building was of wood and the
fire spreadpwith great rapidity. The chill
dren were hastily aroused and hurried
from the building wrapped in their night
clothes and bed-quilts. All were badly
frightened and when the shrieks of those
who were being cremated in the roaring
mass of flames reached their ears they
became almost unmanageabIe, and were
with difficulty prevented from rushing
into the fire in an attempt at rescue.


The building was soon destroyed and at
daylight the work oil searching the ruins
was taken up. All the children were &C.
counted for by noon. The home was ten
miles from Dallas and it would have been
impossible to get aid out in time had it
been asked for. The matter Will be inves-
tigated.

a sickly-looking white infant under her
care. apparently for no other reason than
that the baby tossed aside its coverings
a half hour later. on my return. the girl sat
talking with another nurse maid, and still
pounding the cab up and down: the little
one under the blankets was quiet. thor.
oughly cowed and submissive. Another
scene In Lafayette Square A negro girl
having In charge two beautifully dressed
children-a girl about ten years of age and
a boy OF two or three-stopped near one of
the benches not far distant from wbera
sat. The little boy seemed tired and fret
ful. In sudden burst Of rage the girI
seized him by the shoulders, and literaIIv
damned the child down on the hard bench

soundly slapped her cheek thus cutting off
any revelations to the mother when the
children reached home. Such scenes. of
more frequent occurrence than we realize

given responsibility, deliberately puts aside
the afternoon nap the social visit the fas-
cinating art work, and. either in person. or

reefs her babe, sleeping and waking.

Mrs. Esther Nelson took q bottle Of alcohol to
her room on the second floor ut 5o4 West Twen-
ty-flrst street yesterday to use in cleaning a
bedstead. The room was dark, so she lighted q
candle. Directly she took the cork out Of the
bottle the alcohol exploded and was scattered
over the room.


Her three children we're in the room, the oldest
nearly ready to go to school. Some Of the burn
ing fluid fell on tho two-year.old girl. Eugenia.
The child ran screaming into q corner and tried
to beat the flames out with her feeble hands.
Mrs. Nelson's clothes blazed up and the bedding
caught fire. The alcohol ran over the floor,
trailing fire in all directions. The children hud-
died in n corner, half dead with fright.


The mothers and the baby's screams brought
the other tenants TO the door. but instead of
rendering aid they ran wildly about calling for
help, until Mrs. Minnie Jarman came from the
Nat opposite the Nelson's. She ran straight into
the burning flat, flung the burning bedclothing
out of the window, threw n blanket about Mrs.
Nelson, and beat out the fire on the child's cloth
ing. Then she hurried the other children out.
When the firemen came there was only the burn
ing furniture to attend to.


Mrs. Nelson was badly burned. but she would
not allow the police TO take her to the hospital.
The baby's injuries were slight. But for Mrs.
Jarman's presence of mind the whole family
might have persisted.

A tornado struck halfmile east Of the VII
lage Of Valley Stream. Long Island. yesterday
afternoon and wrought considerable damage.
A hotel was almost totally wrecked, the upper
part Of another building carried away. big
trees were dragged from the earth and scattered
long distances. part of a big wagonshed disap-
peared. and a horse was lifted into the air ana
carried a considerable distance.


The tornado started at about 3:2o o'clock. near
the steamboat dock at Seaside Rockaway
Beach. There were three distinct waterspouts
within a few minutes Of each other in Jamaica
Bay. One formed near the steamboat dock ana
was the largest and most severe. The others
confined themselves to the bay The water or
the largest one was carried in pillar across
Rockaway Point, and then continued on across
the bay and the swamp lands. sucking water
from the bay. This went to pieces short dis
tance from the railroad trestle and re-
markable sight. Before it broke the water had
been sucked into the air to the distance Of two
hundred feet according to the estimates made
by some of the witnesses, and to half that dis
tance according to others. Those who give the
smaller distance say that above the water there
was a cloud forming. and that this was what
led the others astray. The base of the spout
was about acre in extent.


The hotel building which wrecked be-
longed to Herman Bohmlen. He is at present
In Germany. It was leased by Charles Noble
With him lived his wife and four children, and
his mother Mrs. Mary Huntington. The hotel
was frame structure two and a half stories
high and was about 100 by - feet 1t faced
the Hampstead Road and Franklin-ave There
only four persons in the hotel when the
wind struck it. They were Mr.. Noble his
mother, one Of his children and man named
Mott, with whom Mr. Noble was bargaining for
the purchase Of horse. The men sat in the
barroom. and were in the act Of drawing up the
papers for the transfer of the animal Mrs
Huntington in the kitchen and the child
was with her. The first they knew Of the storm
when they heard the Of the wind.


The storm struck the building on the west eX.
posure. The first caper Of the wind was to tear
the piazza from its resting place and lift IT into
the air 1t was lifted almost whole straight up
and over the roof Of the hotel, and then dropped
a mass of wreckage on the east side Of the build
ing Then the hotel lifted from its brick
foundation and blown fourteen feet from its old
base.


The wrenching the building received tore al
most every particle of plaster from the walls
and buried the furniture under heaps of lime
and mortar Mr.. Noble says that everything
became black, there was a terrible CRASH, anu
then it appeared though the floor under his
feet was rising and falling. Mott fell 10 the
floor and lay there. When the building. with
many creaks and groans from the strainng tim
bers at last became stationary. both men rushed
from the building.


Mrs Huntington. who in the pantry, re-
ceivad two severe scalp wounds. heavy iron
pot was thrown from its fastenings and cut her
scalp badly. The child was thrown from the
chair on which 1t was sitting and fell on the
floor Both woman and child were covered with
plaster The woman carried TO the house
of Richard Abrams.


The horse for which Mott and Noble were bar
gaining stood in the wagonshed. The shed was
picked up by the wind and carried fifty yards
and then wrecked. portion Of it could not be
found last night, and is supposed to have been
sucked into the vortex and carried into the air.
The horse and wagon were lifted into the air
and then dropped to the ground fifty feet from
where they had been standing. The wagon was
demolished and the horse injured internally.


There landed against the side of the hotel dur
ing the storm a cherry tree Of good size. 1t mad
been pulled from the ground, roots and all
Every bit Of earth was washed from the roots
bv the twisting the tree received in the cloud.
and most of the leaves were stripped from the
branches The tree landed with the limbs down
and the roots sticking up in the air and leaning
against the wrecked hotel The house of Her
man Wichem to the east OF the hotel was also a

Lord Hertford's Haste at the Funeral.
From the London World.


The Lord Hertford who formed the Wal
lace collection. visited Ragley, the family
place In Warwickshre, only once in his life,
and that was on the day of his fathers
funeral. in March. 1912. The third marquis
had died in London. at Dorchester House.
and the body had been brought by road to
Ragley. where it lay in state in the dark
ened dining room, with tall candles burning
all around. the room hung with black
velvet, the bier surrounded by mutes and
piumes while the coronet was displayed on
crimson cushion placed upon the coffin,
and the star and ribbon of the Garter were
on purple cushion. 'Squires. parsons,
yeomen and country folk were all as
sembled. and. having refreshed themselves
the hour arrived fors the funeral in Arrow
Church.


The following account is from volume
printed many years ago for private clrcu-
lation: Just then a travelling Carriage
with four smoking post horses dashed up
the avenue. A solitary traveller got out,
and, looking round him unconcerned, en-
tered the house Of death. This was the
new Marquis Of Hertford. heir to a most
princely heritage. The travel-stained horses
remained standing before the principal
service was being hurried over and the un-
hallowed remains of q man who had left
none to mourn for him were deposited In
the damp. dark vault Then. when the
coffin was consigned to Its niche in the.
family sepulchre. the traveller. drawing his
ample cloak somewhat closer, stepped back
into his carriage and FASTENED away. The
wondering rustics who looked through the
closed windows from treetop and branch at
the Comfortably muf!led figure reported
that he had fallen asleep before he reached
the park gates. But, asleep or awake, none.
of them ever looked, again on the impassive-
face of their landlord"

The piano was old Steinway grand.

| first touch convinced him that the notes

Now, it happened that in all the months

dCstrously built themselves a home i'm the
shape of a nest large a good-sized
saucer. The soft p:anissimo prelude to tho
selection gently woke the wasps from their
sweet dreams. But when the soft pedal

and the piano began to reverberate TO the
heavier passages the disturbed wasps sus-
pected danger. They curled their backs
and stretched and shook their gauZy wings

the fact that the music, far from soothing
the savage breast of the vicious wasps
ambushed within that piano, rousing
their he, played on. From pianissimo to

while the wasps fiuttered their wings wick





fessor played. Now came the climax: now
he was throwing together vast handfuls OF
notes i'm the basso profundo region of the
Instrument. Just as the Steinway grand
was belching forth from its innermost soul
the musical thunder of that great Wagne-
rian opera, the vengeance-hunting army of
yellow jacket wasps swept out of the belch-
ing instrument, with buZzing war song,
DOWN the hallway and upon the audience.
Suddenly soul-rending shrieks resounded
through the hall. Men and womsn were

town and sat down on the railway track.
They we're the stereoptico-musical aggre-
cation of San Antonio, and their faces. as
they recounted the horrors through which
they had passed, were the image of that OF
Napoleon on the night of Waterloo. They
tagged the south-bound passenger train
and took passage for San Antonio Their

steel tire slipped from one Of the driving

TO Keep 1t on the rail, and try, with that
big connecting rod rising and falling two

broken tire rolling eighty feet every
second, to make the tire fall of the wheel
and over the connecting rod, so 1t shall
drop clear Of the wheel, the rod, the rail

William Hoey was one of the best

old-nme partners decided to revive "a

condition marked him as a victim of
paresis, and he gradually failed.

ed to walk the entire distance Very

road yelling. When the procession had

text:
LONDON, Eng, Jan. THE libel suit
brought by Earl Russell against his
mother in-law, Lady Scott, and two male
defendants, John Cockerton, an engineer,
and William AyIott, a valet, came to
most sensational ending to-day when the
defendants pleaded guilty. The case has
been exceedingly nasty in character, but
involved people OF such high rank that it
has attracted wide attention, and the
court has been crowded at every session
with those eager to hear the testimony
against the Earl.


AS the case progressed, however, 1t be-
came evident that the defense was very
weak one. The defendants did rot deny
making the assertions complained Of but
claimed that the statements concerning
the Earps misconduct were true. The evil
dence they introduced, however, failed to
sustain the charges.


Yesterday the court was crowded, as it
was known that counsel for the defense
was to sum up. The counsel contended
that Lady Scott's whole object was simply
to vindicate her daughter and defend the
latter from her husband s attacks.


The counsel for Lady Scott. continuing.
said the defendant still believed the state
ments made by the male defendants were
true, and he secuted the idea that nara
tives were invented, pointing out the
progressive step of Earl Kusselrs career
at Oxford, the incidents of 1887, claiming
they strongly tended TO confirm the stories
of indecencY.


During the latter portion or the sum-
ming up of the counsel for the defense
Lady Scott burst into tears and counsel at
the close of his remarks was applauded,
after which the case was adjourned Tor the
day.


This morning the courtroom was, if pos
sible, more crowded than yesterday, and
the spectators were rewarded with the sem
sation tina. they had been expecting since
the first days of the trial. When the court
had been opened for business and the pris-
oners had been brought III Solicitor Wal
ton arose and announced that under the
advice of counsel the defendants withdrew
the plea of justification in uttering libels
com planned of by Earl Russell and pleaded
guilty as charged. The announcement
created profound sensation.


Lady Scott was in highly excited,
almost hysterical condition, and seemed a
times as if she were about to faint. The
other defendants, Aylott and Cockerton,
maintained an air OF nnconcern.


Under the circumstances there was no
need for further trial. The jury rendered
formal verdict of guilty, and the
Court announced that sentences would
be imposed tomorrow. What the sem
fences will be is a matter of much
discussion and surmise. 1t is generally
believed that Lady Scott's action was
based on desire to take her daughters
part, and that she was really deceived by
the male defendants. If the court takes
this view her sentence will probably be
light one. The punishment of the two
men will doubtless be more severe.


The present case grew out of an equally
sensational and even more disgusting case
brought in 1891, when Countess Russell,
daughter of Lady Scott. sued for divorce
from Earl Russell, making accusations
against her husband of a most revolving
character. The case was bitterly con-
tested, and attracted great attention. 1t
ended in the failure of the Countess to
prove her charges and denial of the di-
vorce asked. Subsequently the Earl APP
piled for divorce and was granted it.
At the trial Lady Scot; and the two other
defendants in the present case made the
most damaging kind of statements con-
corning the conduct of the Earl, and it
was these statements that led to the pres
emit libel suit

BRIDGEPORT, Conn, July 22.-Two
masked burglars, who had been fright
ened early this morning into an clubhouse
OF George Nichols, wealthy farmer liv-
ing at Daniels Farm, village in Tair-
field County, returned to the house fifteen
minutes after their scare, burst in the
door, from behind which they could see
Nichols and his sister still searching for
them, and without warning shot them
both. They forced the sister 10 tell where
$500 was concealed and took that. They
loaded the table in the dining-room with
cakes and liquors, aud sat with the dying
farmer and ate, drank and made merry.
They ever fed brandy ana water to him.
They ransacked the house, and finally,
two hours after their first visit, went
away promising to leave word with q
neighbor that doctor was needed.
Farmer Nichols died shortly after they
left. His sister, though terribly wounded,
may recover.


The crime resembles in many respects
another robbery and murder within three
miles of the Nichols house. Nichols and
his sister lived alone in the house. He
was 63 years old and she 81. They had
accu ~ ulated fortune of from S1Oo, 900 to
$3.50, OOO and much money was Kept In the
house. Nichols was aroused by noise al

made complete search of the premises.
Tney had barely returned and bar red the
kitchen door when the two men broke it
down. The next instant there were two
pistol shots. Nichols fell fiat on the floor.
Mary Nichols felt sting in her right side.
In moment her right arm, which held
the light, became paralyzed and the lamp
dropped TO the floor, leaving the place in
darkness.


The robbers struck light and carried
the dying farmer to a rocking chair. One
OF the robbers sat down in chair beside
him, while the other one, pistol In hand,
walked up the back stairway after the sls-
ter, who had staggered into her bedroom.
BY string of profane threats he forced
her 10 reveal the moneys hiding place.
Then he returned to his companion who
was watching the old man. The woman,
summoning her whole strength, crept to

robbers caught her and carried her TO bed.
They politely obeyed her request for cam
phor and water. A large portion OF the
couples fortune, deeds and other docu-
ments were searched for, but left behind.
Then, after leisurely feasting, the robbers
de parted.


1t was nearly 8 o'clock, seven hours
alter the shooting, when Miss Nichols,
creeping along on her hands and knees,

about o'clock this morning.


Johnson and Joiner. according to the
confession of the former. were guilty of
the murder of five mem bers of the Cotton
family some time ago. Williams was
awaiting trial for numbering his wife.


Early in the night, when it became
known that John Johnson and Arch
Joiner, charged with the Cotton family
murders, would be lynched, groups of
strangers from every section of this and
adjoining parishes began to arrive. They
held low conversations on the street cor
ners. The night was most miserable
one, rainy and gloomy.


About o'clock there were perhaps 250
people on the street, when suddenly some
$50 men on horses galloped up to the jail,
and having found the deputy who had
charge, forced him to open the Jail door
and also open the steel cages. They then
took from the cages the three colored
men. The mob made no hostile demon
strations. After procuring their men they
held short consultation and decided to
hang Gus Williams to an oak tree near
the negro church, on the outer edge of
town. A rope was quickly adjusted over
a large limb with one end around VIII
ligms' neck. Williams was made to get
on horse. The horse was struck with
whip and jumped from under Williams.
His neck was broken and his body was
jerked down.


Williams disposed of, the crowd started
on the long march to John Cotton
house, where the murders were COM
mitted. The distance travelled was twelve
miles, through heavy rain. There were
nearly 200 in the crowd during the march.
Arch Joiner prayed a great deal, but
Johnson was quiet and sullen.


After four hours the Cotton residence
was reached, and all dismounted. Joiner
made a desperate break for liberty, but
was captured before he had gone very far.


Joiner and Johnson began curs;ng each
other, and asked permission from the
crowd to settle their dispute in prize-ring
style, which was granted.


The fight lasted about five minutes
Johnson, although the smaller man, had
considerably the Test of the fight when





They were then taken into the Cotton
house and efforts were made to get full
confession from them. John Johnston
stuck to his former statement that Arch
Joiner was the man who committed the
murders.


Joiner stoutly maintained his innocence
for a while, but finally confessed that he
killed Mrs. John Cotton, Miss Agnes Mil
ler and Miss Lizzie Miller. a discussion
then arose as to the best way to dispose of
the murderers.


Some were in favor of burning them,
and fires were made for that purpose; but
better judgment prevailed, and 1t was
finally decided to hang them. This was
done, and their bodies riddled with bull
lets. 1t was Arch Joiner's earnest request
that he be shot to death, and this was de-
cided upon as the mode of death to be
meted out to Joiner; but at the last
moment, after the fire had been started, it
was urged that he be hanged, as Gus Will
liams had been. They were taken half
mile from the Cotton residence and
strung up. They both implicated two
other negroes. All is quiet now.

storm between and o'clock this morn

serious washouts along the main line of the

City depot nearly an hour late. At Carl
stadt the water from the hills washed sand

moved.

between Carlstadt and Jersey City were
submerged. and the trains had to run very
slowly The tracks west of the Bergen

at one time several of the inward-bound

were flooded. There was bad washout
on the Erie railroad near the Passaic
bridge. The tracks were carried away, and
there were no trains between $40 and $50
between Rutherford and Passaic.


The Railway river rose eight feet higher

feet higher than when the big storm oc-
CURED four weeks ago. The lowlands
about Railway were flooded, and consider
able damage was done. There were fears
that the Irving street bridge at Railway
would be carried away, but it stood the
strain. Boats were in use to cross streets
in the lower section of Railway, where in
places the water was four and five feet
deep. People living in the streets near the
river were taken out of the second floors
of their residences today. as the water was

the front doors


The water from the river backed up to
Irvington and Hamilton streets to a depth
of fifteen feet. Water in the Regina Music
Box Company building was four inches
higher than the main floor, where much
stock was kept.


At Atwood bridge, four miles from Ran

kiln and caused loss of $4,000.

ST. JOHNS, N. F., April 27.-The
French barkentine Victor Olgene arrived
at st. Pierre Miquelon bringing survivors
of the brigantine Valiant, Captain Pierre,
which struck an iceberg on the Grand
Banks ON the night of Wednesday, April
IA, and sank within twenty minutes.


The survivors believe their sixty.nine
comrades perished. Their ship was nearly
four weeks out from st. Malo, when, with
out an instant's warning, she struck full
speed against a low.lyi ing iceberg. Her
stem and bows were split to pieces and
the hold was speedily flooded. Many of
those aboard were drowned outright by,
the inrushing waters or crushed by falling
timbers as they tried to reach the deck.


The ship was en- her way from France
to st. Pierre for bait to begin the summers
codfishing on the banks, and was carrying
fifty fishermen to join the st. Pierre fleet.
She had altogether seventy-three persons
aboard. After the collision those who
reached the deck. mostly clad in night
obes, realizing the ship was soon to sink,
wildly began to launch the dories. The
boats, being insufficient for all, a brutal
scramble for places in them ensued. The
rescued dory was one of the first to clear
the snip.


The survivors are ignorant of how many
others got away, but fear very few, be-
cause the ship sank within twenty min
utes, and the screams which accom- panied
her disappearance proved only too clearly
how many were carried down to death.
The rescued dory had seven men aboard
when she left the ship. Only one, Gren-
Vile, the boatswain, was fully dressed,
and the party pushed off in such haste
that they neglected sails. oars, provisions
or water. For four days they were adrift
in this frail craft every sea sweeping
over them, drenching them to the skin
ana forcing them to continuous balm 2,
until they were too feeble to throw out
any more water, and careless whether
they perished or not they packed them
selves closely along the boats bottom for
warmth. But the keen frost and the sur
rounding icebergs and foes rendered
warmth impossible, and hunger soon
added its terrors. Death cut short the
sufferings of two of them on the second
day. A few hours later they sighted the
Captains boat also without oars, drifting
with half dozen occupants. She re-
ported that one of the party was already
dead, and as none of the rest had since
been heard Of il is believed all were lost.


The boats soon drifted apart. The next
day Grenvllle's boat lost third man by
death. That night the famished survi-
vors ate the flesh from the corpse. The
next evening when the party was rescued
the body was almost half eaten. So raw
enous had they become that Captain Eve
and crew of the Victor Olgene, which res
cued them a week ago yesterday. were
Mortified at the sight and sank the body
and boat at once.


The four living men were all bereft of
reason and so exhausted that they had to
be hoisted over the ships side swathed IN
blankets, their bodies being masses of
FROST bitten flesh. When found they were
all lying unconscious in the bottom with
six inches OF water surrounding them and
could not stand or speak for days. When
they reached st. Pierre tonight they had
to be carried ashore on stretchers. Their
limbs are useless, and amputation is
necessary upon every one. This work was
begun by the doctors tonight 1t is an.
nounced that three may recover, but the
fourth cannot live. Even if the others

Dowan Young's search for his slave sister,

Miss Moss" Later she married Reeves,

support.


Although forty-one years old. Susie
Young-she is known by both names-is
spry and active. very straight and a good
worker. She has q few rooms in Cottage
Lane, where she and her daughters live,
and they are kept clean and neat. The
whole lane likes the family and rejoices
with 1t over the reunion which seems so
certain to come.

ROME, Oct ia monster procession Of 3d.
600 merchants and shopkeepcrs paradod the

proposed income tax. A deputation represent

lister. the Marquis di Rudini, and formally pre-

Atter the procession had marched over Its pro-
scribed route Anarchists took advantage Of the
occasion to start a riot, which assumed q very
serious character before 1t was ~quelled. The
rioters wero armed with sticks, stones, and re-
v%olvers. and used these weapons effectively.
Troops were called out to put down tho dis
turbance, but the rioters turned upon tho sol.
diers and fought them desperately. Several Of
the troops were wounded and ono workingman
was killed. Order was finally restored and q
number Of arrests were made.


In consequence OF tho riot the Project has

The city this afternoon presented q remark
able aspect. All the shops and even the cafes
were closed, printed notices on the shutters say
ing that they had been closed for fiscal reasons.


Tho streets leading to tho Capitol were
throngod with enormous crowds. The commit
tee that headed the procession included the
Mayor and the President of tho Board OF Trade.


Having regard for the responsibility Of the
demonstration, the Marquis di Rudini. Prime
Minister and Minister Of the interior, had not
ordered any special police precautions. Doubt
less the organizers OF the demonstration In
tended 1t to DO orderly and digniied. and did

As soon as tho procession started the latter

who numbered only forty. soon received rein.
forcemcnts. A squad of gendarmes arriving

The shouts changed to Down with tho bay

and struck with fists. When the troops ar

and there was moro stoning.


A refuse cart passing, some OF the mob

upon the troops and gendarmes. The cart
was smashed into fragments. which were used
as weapons. Soon the entire street was a mass
OF nghtlng humanity. knives and reyolvers
were freely used. More troops were hurried to

Although the violence was primarily due to
the law!ess element, the affair Is significant,
and will cause the Ministry to reflect. The

CHICAGO, ILL.,, Feb. .27.-Fred Schineer,
the Bohemian and resident of this city,
won the six-day bicycle race st latter
Sails, which ended tonight at 1905
o'clock. The final contestants and the
distances they covered were as follows:


Schineer, 17SS miles 4 laps; Miller of
Chicago, 1764 miles 1 lap; Ashinger, 1927
miles; Lawson, the Terrible Swede," 1907
miles 1 lap; Hanson, 1903 miles laps;
Iliff, the legless rider, 461 miles.


There was no exciting finish for the
thousands of people in the sitting build
ing to go into ecstacies of delight and
make an uproar over. The contest prac-
tically terminated at 8 o'clock tonight.
Miller was then twenty-six miles behind
the winner, and Ashinger, the veteran
rider OF long distances, had thirty-six
miles to gain on the second-place man.
Miller was physically unequal to close
the distance gap in the final hour set for
the racers to drop out, confident that
Ashinger could not get the best of him.
Schineer was glad of the chance to quit
and retain his grip on the $1,000 purse, and
one by one the half-dozen half-dead rae
ers dropped from their wheels and sought
their quarters.


For time the mass Of spectators had
nothing to do except listen to the music
and gaze at the empty track. Feeble in
terest was revived by the temperance of
the prize winners, who did few sleepy
turns, looking more like men in a trance
than contesting professional athletes.
Exhausted in body and mind the riders
quickly sought their couches. They were
rewarded for their brief return by being
made the recipients of liberal applause
and bouquets of flowers. Miller and Schi-
neer, the two Chicagoans. made theatrl-
cal display of their intention to call it
race by riding around arm in arm and
bearing some of their floral tributes. Law
son and Ashinger came out and did the
same act.


The next diversion came when the stair
way leading from the bridge over the
track fell beneath its load of human
freight. The fall was not enough to more
than brulse those who were caught, but
there was intense excitement for a few
minutes. City building inspectors and
the police found it necessary to clear
away the dangerous wooden superstruc-
lures, which were of the Eghtest construc-
ton.

Little land SO great of heart,


Midst world so abject grown
Must thou play thy glorious part,

FRESNO, CAL, Aug. Gilbert Partee,
an 11-year-old boy, at an early hour this
morning shot and instantly killed Rich
ard Griffin, who had invaded the Partee
home and viciously attacked Mrs. Carrie
Partee, the boys mother. All parties to
the tragedy, which occurred in the west
ern portion of the city, are colored.


Griffin had been friend of Partee and
his family for some years. Some time
ago, when Mrs. Partee went away from
the city, she left Griffin to guard the
house. At about l o'clock this morning.
Griffin went to the Partee home, and,
humping upon the cellar door, demanded
admittance. Mrs. Partee asked him what
he wanted and he told her that he wanted
his clothes. She reminded him of the I'M
seasonable hour and told him to go away
and come in the morning. He said he
wanted to leave early this morning.
Thereupon young Partee. who, with Miss
Eliza Baker, was with his mother, opened
the door and handed him a lighted lamp.
Mrs. Partee told Griffin that he would find
his clothing in the cellar.


The fellow took the lamp and went into
the cellar, where he remained for twenty
minutes or more. All the while he was
in the cellar he was most profane and.
made great noise. He then demanded
admIttance upstairs, and on being refused
became very violent. Mrs. Partee finally
went to the door and declared she would
shoot him if he did not go away. He
threw the lamp at her and also q handle
less hammer and swore he would kill
them all. Neither the lamp nor the
hammer hit the woman, and she shot
into the floor TO scare her assailant.


Griffin then rushed upon the woman
like tiger and threw her back upon the
bed. They rolled off to the floor, the
woman falling face downward and Griffin
pinning her down with his knees and
resting his full weight upon her. He
choked her and fercely bit her on the
neck, leaving the imprints OF two sets of
teeth In her flesh.


In the rush he had secured the pistol,
for the possession of which a struggle now
ensued. Miss Baker seized his left arm
and the boy the right hand, securing the
pistol. Mrs. Partee was shouting, Don't
shoot" fearing the boy might kill her.


The nerves of that lad were too steady
for that, however. He watched his
opportunity and sent two bullets into
Grifin's body just below the shoulder
blades. Griffin released his victim, arose
and ran out. He soon changed his mind
and was coming back when the boy fired
two more shots, both taking effect in the
lett SIDE one in the region of the heart
and the other in the left lobe of the liver.
Griffin fell dead few feet from the door


The brute who so deservedly met death
was a strapping fellow and 35 years of
age. The Corouer's jury exonerated the
lad.

council tonight passed an ordinance levy

special taxes paid on street paving. When

levied on the abutting property. Some Of
the owners made the first payments,
amounting in the aggregate to $4,000;
others refused and were sued, the cases
appealed and the special tax levy declared
by the higher courts to be illegal. Those
who paid have sought reimbursement,

notice that he would veto the ordinance.

ALDEN, June 29.-The Indian govern
ments steamer Mayo. sent out in search
of the missing steamer Alden, from Yoko-
hama, on April ., via Colombo and Alden.
for London, which was last heard OF when
leaving Colombo on June 1 for this port

Alden was totally lost off the Island OF
Socotra, at the eastern extremity of Africa
on the morning of June 8.


The Alden carried thirty-four passengers
from China and Japan.


The captain of the wrecked steamer.
some of her officers and crew and seven
white passengers were swept overheard
and drowned very soon after she ran
ashore. Eight lady passengers, nine chill
crew succeeded in getting away from the
wreck, but they have not been heard of
since, and little hope, owing to the bad
weather which has since prevailed. is en-
tertained of their safety.


The Mayo saved nine of the Aden's pas
sengers and three of the white and thirty
three OF the natives of the steamers crew.
All OF these persons were rescued just as
the Alden was breaking up. The survivors
Of the wrecked steamer were brought to
this port by the Mayo and are being cared
for by the local authorities.


In all, the drowned and missing include
twenty-five passengers, twenty European
officers and thirty-three natives of the
Aden's crew.

States monitor Puritan, which left Charles
ton last Friday and encountered heavy
weather all the way up the coast, is now
in Raleigh Bay, near Durants life-saving
station in disabled condition, and the
cruiser Columbia has gone to her assist

was obliged to anchor in Saturdays s

bled and that she could make but little
headway against the heavy sea.


After an exceptionally slow trip. how
ever, she arrived off Hatteras late Tues
day evening, when it was discovered that
the other engine was working badly. The
Puritan steamed back and forth in front
of the life-saving station, signaling her
condition to the lie savers, who patroied
the beach all night SO as to give immedi-
ate aid should it be required. Captain
Bartlett managed to keep off shore all

he wired the Navy Department that one

Miss English opened in the affirmative.
She advocates abstinence from all stirnu-
lants, including tea. coffee and meats. and
moderate diet Of grains, vegetables and
fruits, carefully selected with reference to
individual needs; pure air, ample exercise.
thorough bathing, a clear conscience, a
cheerful disposition and an absolute faith
In the supremacy of mind over matter.
She closed with quoting the following rules
from a well-known author: Drink less,
breathe more: eat less, chew more: ride
less, walk more; clothe less, battle more:
worry less. work more; waste less, give
more; write less, read more; preach less,
practice more

acy they maintain over disease and concen-
tration upon the case in hand. She gave
striking illustrations.


Miss Gfllett thought it an even question
as to whether the mind was itself ma
terial or the body spiritual, and gave illus
tratioDs of mental disorder and insanity
from disease, and mental cures from re-
stored physical health.


Miss Holmes had found no mental
panacea for physical suffering, and wished

Miss Saunders had not touched medicine
for ten years: had learned how mental
conditions caused disease. and how their
correction removed it. From fever sore
on the lip to bunion on the foot, all were
removable, durable, preventable by health
full mental action.


Mrs. Snyder most eloquently declared the
control OF the spirit over all human ills.
Evil thoughts poison, good thoughts renew
and give nutrition to the body.


Mrs. Spencer had that morning gone into
the college hau to be reminded by wealth
of fragrance and bloom that sixty years
had gone over her head. She refused to
believe it, and students faced her with two
encyclopedias to prove it. Why, at sixteen

afraid she wouldn't, and now she intended
and expected to live forever 1t all de-
ponds on the point of view. A puny, sickly
feeble child, not considered worth raising,
she had come in contact with q grand
heroic soul that had struck the chords
which awakened the, imprisoned nature
and made it free


She believes that the mind, preceding on
its mission from the great First Cause,
creates and forever recreateS the spirit
ual body. and for earthly uses the mate
rial body. and tenderly nourishes and cher
isheS both. Can we, can the human race
obtain, maintain and retain health? A
thousand times, yes!

selves it would take many generations to

A pair Of big horned owls were nightly visitors

Down at the big cottonsecd oil mills these owls

birds fundamentally in the matter been dis

The night Waterman at the mills who SUPER

and must signal his presence at these various

ness il is to inspect this dial plate each morning

Waterman had slept at his post. and afterward

wrong. and after one or two nights the clerk
informed the manager. and they concluded to
main in the office over night To investigate the
matter. The Waterman seemed to be faithfully

nails came all right


Presently there was a scratching and scram-
bling over the big scales and up on the weighing
shcd lust without the Office window. and three

Rats" said the manager facetlously. as he

There they arc!" called the clerk and on the

OF the darkness each selling rat and twanging
the wire Justify with their big wings click!
click" went the register. and the owls stood ac-
cused and the Waterman was cleared.


The manager told him OF the episode the next
morning and the old man laughed about II and

had impeached his honor SO that night' arm
ing himself with a gum and choosing an auspi-

For a whole week thereafter the other bird

ons with his plants. Finally. one night. the old
man saw the owl tapping and hying about In
a frantic manner. beating his wings against

MONTREAL. Nov. s.-Advices received here
say that the Gaspe oil wells are of wonderful
richness. The wells, which have been closed
down for several weeks, are again open, and the
refneries are working day and night.


For tho past two or three years an English
company, the Petroleum Oil Trust. Limited, has
been carrying on operations with great secrecy.
all tho employees being bound not to divulgo
anything they might learn about the company's
business. SO that it has been very difficult to OBJ
tain anything like complete or reliable informa-
ton. The company owns over $4,000 freehold
acres of oil-bearing lands and of mineral and oil.
bearing, rights in perpetuity, which are free OF
rent and royalties.


All the features which betoken the existence
or petroleum In quantity are found in the PENN.
sula Of Gaspe. Its geographical position and
tho fact of Its being on the seaboard within
seven days of London and 900 miles nearer
European markets than the United States oil
fields give it advantages in the matter Of car
riage and freight. Labor, timber, and fuel are
cheap and abundant, while the climate Is favor
able for petroleum mining all the year round.
It is said that at the lowest estimate
from 1000 to $4,000 wells may be sunk upon
the property. The company has also obtained
grants from the Federal Government OF mining
rights over largo areas in the neighborhood OF
its other properties, thus controlling practically
the whole of the oil.bearing region. The output
from the wells will, 1t is believed, result in
formidable competition with the Standard Oil
Company.

NEW ROCHELLE, July lathe storm which
passed over this place last night was the worst
in many months. Several large trees were
struck by lightning, others were uprooted, and
many electric light and telephone wires were
torn down. The streets were almost impossible.


In Echo Bay yachtsmen were kept busy all
night saving their craft from destruction. Re-
ports from Fort Slocum state that the storm
there was terrific. The yacht Handicap, which
is owned by Capt. Swift, a surgeon at the fort,
broke from her mornings and was swept far out
into the Sound. Sentry Robert Wilson swan
800 yards and caught her. He fell overheard
three times before he was able to run the yacht
ashore. A hole was knocked in her port side.


Defender braved the storm admirably. She
was completely surrounded by masses Of wreck
age this morning. Several Fort Slocum soldiers
went out In boats and pushed the wreckage
adrift.


During the height Of the storm the schooner
Mary went ashore on Harris Island. The crew,
composed of four men, chung to the rigging all
night. They were rescued this morning by two
lumber tugs from Boston.

PoUGHKEEPSIE. n. Y, June 25.-Be-
fore the eyes of the boating world Cornell
won to-day victory so decisive as to
establish beyond doubt or cavil her claim
to recognition among the foremost Ameri-
can colleges in aquatic sports. That Yale
had derided this claim and Harvard had
only grudgingly admitted it made the
victory more glorious. Neither the blue
nor crimson could do well enough to make
the little men from Cornell exert them
selves, and with the other two crews spent
and breathless the winners shot past the
finish line and pulled gayly down the river
for half mile TO their launch ss fresh as
if they were beginning instead OF finish
ing the greatest race in American college
annals Yale finished second, two and a
half lengths behind, and Harvard, with
one man in the bottom OF the boat, barely
crossed the line six lengths further back
before her men collapsed utterly.


Three distinct systems of rooms were
on trial. Charles Courtney had taught
Cornell the short, snappy American
stroke. Uader their old coach, Boz Cook,
whose instructions have pointed the way
of Yale to victory so often, the New
Haven boys learned and faithfully prac-
ticed his combination of English and
American strokes. Harvard relied upon
the guidance of R. c. Lshmann, a Cam
bridge University man, who came to this
country 20 teach the American college the
English stroke. That the result was a
triumph for the American stroke cannot
be denied.


CornelPs shell, under the quick, powerful
strokes of the crew, which was by far the
smallest and lightest in the contest, cut
through the water like knife, with little
of the dragging between strokes which
tells so terribly In long pull.


To Yale the second position was as
bitter as the third to Harvard. Yale was
beaten by an enemy whom for years she
has spurned as unworthy of her steel.
Contempt for the Ithaca men was openly
expressed before the race


1t looked dubious for Cornell at the
start. Springing from poise with swift,
strong start taught them by Lehman,
Harvard got away well in front, with
Yale second and Cornell, furthest from
the western shore, little behind. For a
dozen strokes or more the crimson led
with slow, steady stroke, and the deep
Harvard yell thundered down the long
of sb
Yale took the stage, while the battle-cry
of the sons of Eli smots the hills. There
was not yet any response from the Cornell
crew. Harvard led her by more than q
quarter of length. But the little Cor
nell cockswain knew what he was doing
From the bank the short, piston-rod
swing of the bodies seemed the same. but
at each swing the shell pushed forward a
little on the rivals. At the half-miIe the
three keen prows were aligned. Pande-
monium reigned on shore, three college
yells merging into cataract OF cIamor.


For fully 25o yards the crews struggled
along, first one and then another leading
until grad ually the Cornell men began to
hold slight advantage. Then they shot
the front of their shell about fifteen feet
ahead of the Yale bow and kent it there


This was the beginning OF the end and
from that point until they crossed the fin
ish line the Cornell men were never
headed. With superb style The Ithacans
swept along, the crowds sending forth
volIeys of encouragement and joy. At
the mile and quarter post the Yale crew
shot past the cambridge eight and began
a long, stern chase after the flying Cor
nellians.


AS the mile and half post was passed
Cornell had a length 20 spare and was
rowing 36-stroke.


There was another spurt by Yale. the
stroke going up 10 thirty-seven, but Har-
ward, although left in the rear, lowered
the stroke from thirty-four to thirty-two.
They finished in the order named. Time,

VIRGINIA, NEv., Feb. PA mining
accident, attended with details OF excep-
tlonal horror, occurred at the Savage mine
about o'clock this afternoon Frank
Monahan, well-known and respected
miner. met with an awful death.


With two companions, Dennis Sullivan
and w. H. Thomas, Monahan was en-
gagged in repairing the shaft between the
400 and 500 level. The men stood on
platform OF two-inch planks placed across
the shaft. Ordinarily but one platform is
used, but the awful accident which oc-
Cured in the same shaft just month ago,
when William Byrne was killed, had the
effect of inspiring unusual caution among
shaftmen, and they had an extra platform
placed below the one on which they were
working in order 10 catch them should
they Iall.


They had finished with one set of tim
bers and were raising the lower platform
about five feet above their heads, with the
intention OF repairing the part OF the shatt
Just overhead, when Monahan sprang to
one side 10 make room for the last plank
TO be raised. He lit with apparently
secure footho!d upon one OF the tlmbers
just inserted in the side of the shaft, but
moment later his two companions were
horrited TO see him pitch forward and dis
appear through three-toot opening IN the
platform into the black abyss below.


Monahan's companions Immediately
gave the signal TO hoist and were taken to
the top, where they were joined by the
foreman, and descended into the shaft to
search for Monahans body. They found
it at the S50-foot level, 335 feet below the
platform from which Monahan had fallen.
A few planks had been placed across the
shaft at this place and Monahan had
fallen on them. His body was horribly
mangled. Not a bone was left unbroken,
the top of his head was gone, his nose was
broken, and through great gaping
wound in the back both kidneys dropped
out as soon as his clothing was removed.


Monahan was a highly respected ana
popular citizen. He was prominent in
silver party politics and represented
Storey County in the State Assembly
some years ago. He was native of Ire
land. aged about 45, and leaves widow
and five children.

A smooth, white sheet OF ghoStly snow
The rough, dark stems defines,
All family crossed with row on row
Of shadows from the pines
Amidst the dim, tall arches grand
King Silence reigns profound,
And shuns with night hand clasped in hand,
The agony of sound.
The lingering moon sinks low and dim,
Its time of labor done,
And nature pauses, cold and grim,
And waits the morning sun.
At last its banners bright appear


Along the eastern sky,
Night shoulders, turns with abject fear,
And knows tits time to fly.
The smooth, white sheet is crushed and torn
Where soft the shadows lay,
And on the air harsh voices borne


Proclaim the waking day.
King Silence's frosty calm is broke


BY steady, ringing blows,
A loud duet of stroke and stroke


That quickens at the close.
Destruction reigns throughout the glade
Where spring the ordly trees,
Long years have cast their somber shade
Or whispered to the breeze,
That caught the sunlight's gliding touch
Or jewels of the snow,
Have felt the storm tlend's savage clutch
That hurled them to and fro.
Alas the storm hath spared in vain,
For man assails his crown;
And swayng, quiverng in pain,


A king falls crashing down.
The moaning, splntering, deaf'ning sound
Re-echoes far and wide,
Proclaiming with its last rebound


The fall of sylvan pride.
With canking links the trunk is chained,
And through the flying snow,
With creakng iron cables strained,


The trains of timber go.
And so from dawn to dusky night,


mid ring of steel and cheers,
The hand of man with ruthless might
Undoes the work of years.

wounding many.

rested. Five policemen were badly hurt

CHICAGO, Ill, Feb. 20.-Seven explo-
sions of natural gas at o'clock this morn
ing in the engine-room of the Chicago
Chronicle at 164 and 166 Washington
street, badly shattered the basement ana
business Office and injured ten persons
five of them seriously.


The pipes leading from the street sprang
a leak and the explosion was caused by
ignition from electric light wires.


John Mcmillan, the foreman OF the
pressroom, was the most seriously injured
and his recovery in doubtful.


He was blown against the wall and
badly burned. One arm was so badly
crushed that it will probably have to be
amputated. Larry Hardgrave, the en-
gineer, was blown thirty feet and badly
injured internally. John Stenger, press
man, was seriously burned about the face.


John Wheeler, driver for Case & Mar
tin, who was standing in front OF the
Chronicle Office, was blown half way
across the street, and Charles Williams,
who was standing on the sidewalk over
the gaspipe was blown as high as the Sec
ond story of the building and badly in
jured. Matthew Baines, a mailer, was
severely burned.


A few minutes after the explosion flames
leaped through the basement and con-
sumed the business office and destroyed
the Western Union Telegraph Company s
branch Office adjoining. All the wires
leading to the office, including those used
by the United Associated Presses, were
broken.


The editorial rooms of the Chronicle
were flooded by water and badly damaged
by smoke. The force of the shock from
the explosion broke every plate-glass win
dow in the building and tore up the side
walk in front of the office.


The wall separating the pressroom OF
the Chronicle from that of the Journal
was blown down and the water from the
fire engines flooded the presses and
damaged the large stock Of paper.


Horatio Seymour, publisher OF the
Chronicle, estimates the damage at $40 600.
The presses are not damaged, he says, and
the publication of the Sunday morning
paper will not be interfered with.

TACOMA. Oct. 4.-Advices from China give
further particulars Of the great inundation.
Sixty Chinese towns in the district about Pekin
were flooded early in September, driving out
$4,000 people, OF whom over 10000 are esti-
mated to have been drowned. The authorities
in Pekin are directing tho relief measures, and
the people from tho towns nearest the capital
have been permitted to live within the city
walls. Here they have no covering against the
rain, which Is still falling. and great efforts are
necessary to provide them with food. Many
citizens OF Pekin have joined the authorities in
this work. The estates Of many Pekin mobiles,
as well as all the crops In the flooded district,
were destroyed.


The rains which caused the floods commenced
late in July and continued until late in August.
Tho Tungchou. Tientsin. and other rivers rose
very rapidly. Some OF them overlooked and
wiped out villages along the banks almost be-
fore the people knew there was any danger.
The magistrates and people in the flooded dis
tricts spent several days praying for dry
weather. Later the officials at Tientsin posted
a proclamation forbiddinR the slaughter Of cattle
and sheep In the hope OF appeasinR the wrath OF
the gods and stopping the rain. Foreign Con-
suls protested against the meat supply being
thus cut Off. asserting that 1t was n violation of
treaty rights.

MONTEREY, CAL. July 18.-The sensa-
tional kidnapping episode in the local
Chinatown last Tuesday night has reached
a new phase and bears flavor of romance.
When the two officers sent in pursuit of
the girl and her captors brought the fugi-
tives back to Monterey last night the story
came to light.


A San Francisco Chinaman whom All
Sigh, the fourteen-year-old daughter of
Monterey fisherman, had once seen took
the youthful fancy of the girl. and as she
was bright and pretty after the Mongolian
type the attraction was mutual. The
suitor offered to buy her from her father,
but Quong Sue, having another prospective
son-in-law in mind, declined to sell her,
and Immediately set afoot negotiations
with the other man. All Sigh did not
wish to marry the man her father pre-
ferred, and so managed in some way to
communicate with her lover. The result
was an offer of $1,000 from the San Fran
cisco man 10 the three men who stole her
for her safe conduct to him. The plans
were laid and all would have gone well
had not some celestial "Peeping Tom"
reported the affair to Quong Sue and thus
started the pursuit.


The runaways were traced from here to
Salinas, but there the trail was lost, and
was only recovered by diligent use of the
wires. The party was finally located in
Watsonville. where officers arrested them,
bringing them TO Monterey last night.


The girl has ever since her capture been
disguised as Chinese boy. The abduc-
tors made such stubborn resis tancs that
it was necessary to handcuff them.


Little All Sigh prefers her San Fran
cisco beau, but .seemed not at all unhappy
over the failure of the plan which was to
give her to him. The hearing OF the case
will come before Judge E. Michaelis to-
morrow.

Old century, tottering to thy rest.
All vainly dost thou beat thy breast:
A new dawn gildS the mountain crest
The glory of thy wondrous day,
With all it's glitter and display,
In twilight shadow dies away,
Almost the poet. in whose rhyme
Thy praise is sung in verse sublime,
Begins his lay "Once on time"
Strange fancies fill thy time-worn brain:
Thou dreamest thou art young again,
With battle cry on land and main.
And dread turmoil of unrest
Embroils the Orient and the West:
Alarms sound at thy behest.
Zen Israel's children, in thy throes,
Imagine DER again their woes;
And many hope toward Zion goes.
The world is mad-men shout and cry
Beholding wonders in the sky,
Renewing faith in prophecy.
Old century, we love thee well.
Thy fame the chronicler will tell
When long forgot thy funeral knell.
To nOb!er action by thee led,
And many high-Souled word was said
New happiness came in thy wake
-Righted was many an old mistake;
An age-worn thirst thy springs did slake
Rest thee-new hopes begin to play:
They drive thy death-born fears away.
And usher in the newer day.
Rest thee, brave requiem shall be thine,
Whose lustrous deeds will long outshine
The strange vagaries of decline.

equal to that encountered yesterday when

while the other children, half starved and
half clothed, ran around the place. The
older children were taken away, but the
aby was left with the mother, for whom

Tacoma, Wash. March 26.-A terrific storm
dashed Puget Sound yesterday. Buildings
blown down and score Of persons injured
but none fatally. Telephone and telegraph wires
were blown down all along the North Pacific
Coast and at Seattle dock picked up by the
wind and carried 200 feet out into the Sound.


At Portland, Ore. the wind at time gained a
velocity Of sixty-iive miles hour. Signs were
blown down. plate-glass windows were broken. and
everything loose was blown in every direction.
Streetcar service also suspended for the great
er portion of the day. owing to trouble with the
wires at oregon City, whence comes the motive
power. The large suspension bridge the
Willamette River II oregon City was wrenched
from its piers fully eighteen inches.

Frank Phillips, the well-known turf

from his scarf.

took and placed the two men under ar
rest. They gave the names of Thomas
Kackie aud Frank Smith, Kackie being
the man who stole the pin.


A crowd gathered round the officer, and
the two prisoners and a man pushed up
to Kackie, held his hand over his mouth
and Kackie. who had the pin in his mouth,
passed it to him. The man who got the

and begged him not to prosecute Kackie
and Smith.


Edner took the two men to the Seven
teenth-street police station, and later they
were conveyed to the City Prison. Yes
terday morning they were booked on the
charge of grand larceny.

CAHTO, CAL. May 3.-The schooner
Nettie Sundborg, Captain o. Johnson
and crew of ten men, from San Fran.
cisco on May 1, is ashore at point near
Hardy Creek. The captain and crew are
safe after having experienced a rather
perilous adventure for time.


The schooner was moored at the Hardy
Creek Lum Der Company's dock last night
preparatory to loading to-day. The
weather indications and the sea were I'M
favorable and Captain johnson had taken
measures 10 assure that the vessel would
n OF break from her moorings during the
night by running two extra lines to the
bow and stern moorings. The schooner
Law at ease until low tide this morning,
wien a succession of heavy swells swept
over her, took away everything movable
from the deck and severed the bowlines.
This permitted the vessel to swing toward
q rocky part of the beach. The sea at this
hour Is o'clock) was running high.


When the vessel broke her moorings
and it became apparent to Captain John
son that he and the crew could not handle
her, all escaped to the rigging for safety.
The schooner was still held by her stern
lines. and it was feared that she would go
to pieces on the rocks if the lines were not
cut. The ca plain and sailors were cling
ing to the rigging, while the heavy sea
was beating over the vessel and all at
tempts to render assistance from the shore
were of no avail.


The captain finally came down from the
rigging with lines entwined about his
body, made his way to the stern and cut
the lines, permitting the vessel to drift
ashore. She landed on the beach, where
she now lies.


The extent of the damage is difficult to
determine. The schooner now shows lit
tie apparent damage, but the continued
rough sea and the high tide tonight will
push her higher upon the beach. Captain
Johnson believes the vessel can be
launched quickly if weather conditions
are favorable. Haymsn & Meyer of San
Francisco are the representative agents.

For six months Chinese slave girl

westbound track.

alighting the ties of the bridge while the train

Sengers that the danger was over.

warded 10 Newark by way OF Elizabeth.


The bridge tenders declare that the accident was
due to loosened rail at the western approach 10
the bridge. None of the passengers were injured
and no damage was done to the engine and cars.

EUREKA, CAL, Jan. 26.-The county
road which crosses the Arcata and Mad

being the scene of another disaster last
evening. John and William Underwood.
brothers, residing on Dows Prairie, were

Blue Lake came into sight and so close

self out of the saddle before his unfor-

train and instantly killed. The horses
body falling under the wheels, almost
derailed the train. William, whose horse
was slower, was enabled to check it in
time, and going to his brothers assistance
found him painfully bruised and cut by
the fall.

Rev. A. East recently told how a dragon

full fed the dull brown eyes Of the larva
become brilliant green like the perfect eyes
within. 1t then crawls laboriously up
some stick or water plant, where 1t estab-
fishes itself firmly. After some ten min
utes to a half hour Of drying the part be-
hind the eyes and above the wing
cases swells and opens. disclosing the
bright green body of the insect. This slow
ly energies. The enormous head, with its
compound eyes. protrudes. the crumpled
wings are drawn from their cases, then one
by one the legs appear. The image now
hangs with the head bent back and the
wings pointing upward. with six segments
of the abdomen exposed, wet and limp
from the dry skin which still clings to its
support by it's stiff and empty legs. After
about ten minutes its legs are strong
enough for the insect, by a quick contrac-
ton of the body, to suddenly lift its head.
and SELLING with its six legs the dry skin
It withdraws the remaining four segments
of its abdomen and hangs by its legs alone.
The wings now begin to expand. They be-
come longer, fiatter and clearer. In a half
hour they show all the beauty Of their
gauzy texture. After about five hours
from first emerging from the water the
perfect dragon-fly is ready for its new life.

RED BLUFF, CAL, July 19.-The fire
has spent its fury and is now under con-
troll. Red Bluff and the country west rest
easy. Probably 200 or 800 men in all went
from town yesterday to the different Sec

dark last evening they began to return.

home. There are two or three places still
being watched, but it is thought that all
danger hes5passed.


Probably not over ten homes were de-
stroyed. A section of territory about ten
by twenty mil es in extent was laid waste
between Saturday morning and last
night, only the residences being saved. A
little grain was burned and much hay in
the stack as well. The larger portion of
the country was covered with timber and
brush and was fit only for grazing. Hun
dreds of cords of wood ready for the m ar
ket and innumerable quantities of stand
ing timber, from which the settlers would
have made their living for years cutting
wood, have been destroyed, and the grass
on the ranges is not only gone, but the
seed which would have made the hills
and dells green next year was burned,

nearly destitute, and it will take the

ana is near Mariei now at the head of the

Albert and Charles Huber, living a few

breeds. and 1t has now been found that
the cross Is very successful, the half-breeds
combining the docility of the domestic AMI.
mails with the endurance and large size OF
the bison. They are also very fine fur pro-
ducers, and grow to maturity in less time
than domestic cattle. The flesh of crossed
animals Is very palatable, and the fur has
all the good qualities of that of the bison.
and Is softer and more silky. The crossed
bloods can stand far more exposure In
winter than can the native cow The
Hubefs believe they have a fortune in theif

HAVANA, CUBA, July 25.-One of the
hottest engagements of the war occurred
Wednesday at Cartagena, Burros and Los
Eununcos, three small villages in the
middle of estates of the same names near
Cienfuegos. The Spanish forces were the
battalion of Saboya and the Cubans were
led by General Alfredo Rego. About
2000 men fought on each side. The Span
iards were going TO attack Cuban hospi-
tai near Los Eununcos, when General
Rego came to the defense. After brief
firing the Spaniards made dash1ng bayo-
net charge on the Cuban vanguard, and
the Cubans retreated. Had it not been
for Rego's courage the fight would have
ended in his utter defeat and the capture
OF the hospital. The Spaniards reached
the hospital ITSELF but there Rego, col
Iecting the men again, ordered machete
charge. The Cubans poured from all
sides upon the SpanIards, and in terri
bic hand-to-hand fight routed the Span
iards.


General Rego declares the Spaniards s
behaved bravely until the order to charge
with machetes was given. Then they
weakened and in their fight left ninety-twc





killed and wounded. The Cuban Iosse.
are officially declared by Rego to be
twenty-four killed and fifty wounded.
The Spaniards lost forty killed and sixty
four wounded.


After the battle Rego. with his we'll
known humanity to prisoners, treated
the Spanish wounded in the hospital they
intended 10 raid. In the hospital before
the fight there were only n few Cuban
soldiers, women ana children. The Span
iards. deceived by their own spies. prob
ably be ieved the hospital of greater i'm
portance. Reso's popularity throughout
the district of Cienfuegos is now very
great. He has resumed operations in the

wounded several times. He is considered
the best horseman in the Cuban army.


After sharp skirmsh with some in
surgents four miles from Yaguaiay, Santa

the hills of Vergara. There they found
the house of a pacifco named Manuel
Luis, They killed LUIS, his brother Ma
tIas, another pacifco named Francisco Es-
pinoso and their wives, i've children and
three other men. After the bodies had
been cut TO pieces the Spaniards placed
them in the house and burned it.


At Sierras Naraniito, Santa Clara prov

Spanish column passed. Some of the

Jacksonville Fla. Jan. "a dispatch from

Cuban coast. was captured by the insurgents
near Cardcnas on Tuesday night. with slight
loss. After securing all the arms and ammuni-
ton on the vessel the insurgents set her on fire
and saw her burn to the waters edge


The Cometa. which was one u the most power
full OF the smaller Spanish vessels in Cuban
waters, had been cruising near Cardenas to pre-
vent the landing of Glibustering expeditions
For some time she had been accustomed to an
Choir at night Of Sierra Morena. The place
where the gunboat anchored was favorable for
an attack from the shore. and the insurgents
determined to capture her Last Tuesday night

Hotchkiss gun. The vessel was struck several

with insurgents left the shore. and the Come;a
was boarded. desperate hand to hand fight
took place on the deck Of the gunboat. the
Cubans using the -nachete with deadly effect
Finally. after the Spanish commander and half
his men had been killed the survivors sur
rendered.

then looted the vessel. securing a quantity of
ammunition. many cutasses and pistols and
few rifles. Two quck-fring cannon which the
gunboat carried were also removed The insur-
gents then fired the boat. which was soon burned
to the waters edge.


When the fate OF the Cometa became known in
Havana the Spanish authorities suppressed the
news and sent cruisers to Sierra Morena When
the cruisers returned their officers reported that
nothing had been seen OF the Cometa The
Spanish authorities then spread the story that
the gunboat had most likely been lost at sea

New lines of worldly meaning in a sweet

The care for others happiness; the gener-

From sordid calculation YOU are drifting


far away,

The participants in wedding celebra-

ceremony. The affair occurred in one of
Birmingham's most thickly populated
suburbs.


The preacher had been notified of the
approaching event and had the church
brilliantly Illuminated. The organist was
there and the happy young couple drove
up in their carriage. The deep tones of
Mendelssohn's beautiful wedding march
filled the sacred ediice and the bridal
party proceeded slowly to the altar. Upon
arriving there they were somewhat sur
prised to find that the preacher was not
present. Naturally supposing that the
reverend gentleman was in one of the
anterooms the couple glanced anxiously
toward the side entrance, but still the
preacher failed to appear.


Several minutes elapsed and the many
friends OF the contracting parties who
crowded the church began to whisper TO
each other about the minister's continued
absence. Still that gentleman failed to
appear, and the expectant couple were
placed in a very EN- barrassing position.
Finally some one went to the pastors
residence, and there they found the
reverend gentleman in the arms OF Nor
pheus. He was awakened and reminded
of the waiting couple.


He hastily arrayed himself and went to
the church, where he performed the cere-
mony that made the young couple hus-
band and wife. The young couple stood
at the altar twenty minutes waiting for
the knot to be tied.


After the ceremony the preacher stated
that he had only recently returned from
the Epworth League convention and was
entirely worn out He had lain down to
rest while awaiting the arrival OF the
party and had fallen asleep. He regretted
the occurrence very much.-Selma Jour-
nal.

text:
A squabble that has caused the with
drawal of one club from the Pacific Inter
club Yachting Association has arisen, and
it is said that the end is not yet. The
trouble began over the regatta of Septem-
ber last. when the McDonough cup was
the main object sailed for and all the
yachts were put in their finest racing trim
in he hope of winning the much-coveted
trophy.


The association was originally composed
of the Pacific San Francisco, CORN THAN,
Encinal and California yacht clubs and its
formation was the result of much hard
study on the part of thos> who have
given the sport the most attention. The
regatta was great event of the year in
yachting circles and each club sent its
fee,est boats, manned by their most e1-
perienced sailors. to com pete.


One of the main conditions governing
the race, which was for sloops not over
thirty feet racing length. was that all
those participating must be amateur
yachtsmen IN the fullest sense Of the word,
and that is where the hitch came.


Among the boats belonging to the San
Francisco Yacht Club the Catherine is
considered crack, and she was sent into
the fray with full confidence that she
would carry off the honors.


She was protested by oiher owners on
the ground that she carried among her
crew professional yachtsman, and the
regatta committee, after hearing testi-
mony and considering the matter, dis
qualified the feet sloop.


Then there was anger among the MEM
bers of the San Francisco Yacht Club and
the majority declared that they woulu
ia in
tons regattas.


The matter simmered for while, the
feeling between the club and the associa-
ton growing stronger the while, until the
annual meeting of The San Francisco
club which took place last month.


|. Cutie was commodore at that time,
and previous 10 the election of officers,
which took place at the gathering, he
offered a resolution to the effect that the
club withdraw from the association and
refuse to longer participate in the regattas.


In support OF his measure he recited the
circumstances under which the Catherine
had been disqualified and denied that her
owners had In any way olated the rules
governing the contest. He characterized
that action OF the regatta committee as
sportsmanlike and petty, and asked the
club to show its spirit by Withdrawing
without delay.


The majority of the members were in
accord with the comm Odore and the reso-
luton was adopted without dissenting
voice. The 1nter-club Association was
notified in short and curt communica-
tion that the San Francisco Club had de-
cided to withdraw from the organization.
No reason for this action was assigned,
but it is perfectly well understood by the
other mem bers of the association and has
intensified the feeling that existed prior
to the withdrawal.


There are some members of the San
Francisco Club who thought the action
hasty, but they are in the minority and
have said little or nothing regarding the
matter.


The San Francisco Yacht Club is the
oldest organization of the kind on the
Pacific Slope and numbers among its
mem bers some of the most enthusiastic
yachtsmen in this City.


Secretary R. R. PHommedieu of the
Inter-club Association, through whose
efforts tue organization was formed, stated
yesterday that the action of the regatta
committee had not been taken hastily
and that the owner of the Catherine had
plainly violated the rules governing the
race by having man on board who had
fallen under the suspicion of being pro-
fessional.


The committee regretted exceedingly
that 1t had been compelled to di-qualify
the sloop, but under the reg ulations there
was no alternative, and to have disre-
garded the protest Of those who claimed
that the Catherine had an outsider on
board would have been to invite still
greater dissatisfaction.
